entry.title: Combined summary - Forwardable Peerswap Incentives, And Closing Surreptitious Communications Tunnels
entry.summary: Forwardable Peerswaps represent a significant advancement in managing liquidity within the Lightning Network, offering substantial improvements over traditional splicing techniques. This protocol stands out by maintaining participant privacy and ensuring that incentive structures are properly aligned. In conventional splicing, service providers may exaggerate their available inbound liquidity, leading to potential transaction failures when actual capacity is insufficient. Forwardable Peerswaps address this by requiring that any inbound liquidity offered must be authentically backed by an equivalent outbound capacity from another node, thereby preventing misrepresentation and promoting transparent and reliable transactions. From a technical perspective, the protocol enhances efficiency in blockchain space usage. While splicing necessitates modifications for every involved channel, resulting in complexity proportional to the number of channels (O(N)), Forwardable Peerswaps reduce this overhead to changes based solely on the swap’s forwarding path, achieving constant complexity (O(1)). This design minimizes block space consumption and simplifies transaction workflows, often reducing them to just two essential onchain Hash Time-Locked Contract (HTLC) transactions: one for creation and one for completion, irrespective of the number of channels traversed. The protocol features three core roles: Initiator, Forwarders, and Acceptor. The Initiator seeks outbound Lightning liquidity and provides onchain funds. The Acceptor receives these funds and supports the new inbound Lightning liquidity, while Forwarders facilitate the connection and are rewarded through rebalancing their own channels without incurring additional onchain fees. To ensure Forwarders are not bypassed, the protocol employs cryptographic obfuscation methods—such as addition modulo and homomorphic encryption—to conceal public keys and hashes. These measures prevent the misuse of these elements as covert communication channels between Initiators and Acceptors that could otherwise undermine the Forwarders’ role and disrupt proper liquidity allocation. Additional safeguards include randomizing key data and carefully managing hash processes, further securing the protocol against exploitation. Certain information, such as transaction amount and timelock duration for the Spilman channel, cannot be fully concealed during peerswaps. The transaction amount carries substantial informational value, potentially exposing the identity of the Initiator. To mitigate risks associated with timelocks, it is recommended to standardize durations to a range of +2012 to +2016 blocks beyond the current height, accommodating negotiation delays while limiting the leakage of identifying details. Regarding onchain fee rates, these can be another channel for sensitive data exposure. By deferring or omitting explicit fee rate communication—initially using zero-feerate transactions and adjusting only if necessary via child transactions—fee rates are prevented from serving as hidden data conduits, thus preserving anonymity. In cryptographic terms, the use of `(e, s)` instead of `(R, s)` is critical to avoid creating unauthorized communication pathways. Utilizing `R` as a value could enable Acceptors to encode their node ID or other information, facilitating direct signaling to Initiators and circumventing Forwarders. Varied scalar values in each zero-knowledge proof ensure that each session remains unique and secure. Shared signing mechanisms such as MuSig2 require both Initiator and Acceptor participation, ensuring that neither party can unilaterally control the resulting signature or transaction, thereby reinforcing protocol integrity. A pivotal element in the hash-exchange process is the concept of “commitment,” which refers to enforceable on-chain actions rather than mere mutual agreement or message exchange. The system mandates that Forwarders will not relay any information, including hashes, until they confirm that the Spilman channel has been established with the correct negotiated value. This approach guarantees that even if an Initiator aborts after making contact with an Acceptor, they have already incurred the cost and effort of opening the Spilman channel, effectively acting as a deterrent against frivolous or malicious behavior. Forwarders prioritize their role as indirect connectors, ensuring that transactions route through them and that they are compensated accordingly. Ultimately, both the Initiator and Acceptor must cooperatively sign transactions that move funds from the Spilman channel into an ordinary Lightning channel, incurring additional onchain fees. This raises important considerations about whether future in-Lightning fees, potentially discounted over time, will outweigh the immediate onchain costs imposed by miners for direct channel openings. Nevertheless, Forwarders provide indispensable value by matching nodes with surplus outbound liquidity to those with inbound demand, justifying their compensation through the requirement that Initiators commit resources up front. Overall, Forwardable Peerswaps introduce a robust, privacy-conscious, and efficient framework for liquidity management in the Lightning Network. Through its innovative structure and rigorous security precautions, it offers a scalable and sustainable foundation for future network operations, overcoming limitations inherent in earlier protocols such as splicing.
